name: Ishikawa (Fishbone) Diagram
use_case: A structured cause-mapping diagram that sorts every candidate cause of a problem into fixed categories — people, process, equipment, materials, environment and measurement — so a group can see the full space of explanations at once instead of committing to the first one. Best used when a defect or quality problem has many plausible contributing factors, several teams each blame a different one, and the discussion needs a shared map before anyone starts collecting data.
strengths: surfaces many parallel causes rather than a single chain
category prompts stop the group from circling one favourite explanation
the finished diagram is a durable artifact for later data collection
works well with mixed groups because every discipline owns a branch
weaknesses: produces breadth without any ranking of which cause matters most
the standard categories fit manufacturing better than knowledge work
large diagrams become unreadable and stall the conversation
risks cataloguing speculation unless each branch is later tested
use_cases: A hospital ward has logged several medication errors this year, and prescribing software, pharmacy supply, staffing and ward layout could each be contributing; the safety group wants every factor laid out before it audits anything.

Attendance at a secondary school has fallen, and staff suggest transport, family circumstances, the timetable and how absences are followed up; the leadership team wants all of these explanations on one page before choosing what data to gather.
About one new account in ten fails to complete onboarding in our software product, and the cause could sit in data quality, integrations, documentation or the handover to support.
Most planning applications reaching a council arrive incomplete, and the form design, the online guidance, the validation checks and applicants' own circumstances might all play a part.
